R&D daily sprint

Meeting records Transcript 
Summary
Amir Houieh presented a concept for an "observant memory" system, initially intended to automatically take notes during therapy sessions to alleviate administrative burden for therapists like Oda, a concept Gabor Kerekes found appealing for its simplicity and potential to address the most tedious work for therapists. This memory system is structured around "learners" which track specific patterns, evolving an "understanding" layer by deciding the relevance of incoming data, a critical feature Gabor Kerekes noted that current LLMs lack, as it requires continuous, guided attention to relevance realization. Amir Houieh confirmed a working prototype with successful testing across three use cases, while Gabor Kerekes suggested packaging the stateful memory system as a CLI tool that can be integrated with Cloud Code's life cycle hooks and recommended using Datastar for building a simple UI.
Details
Therapy Note-Taking Problem and Solution Idea Amir Houieh discussed their therapy session and a problem identified with their therapist, Oda, who spends significant time writing notes, which creates a large cognitive and administrative burden. Amir Houieh proposed an app that listens to the session, analyzes turning points, and automatically takes notes, suggesting this could save therapists, such as those at a clinic of 15 therapists, about an hour and a half per day (00:00:00) (00:06:10). Gabor Kerekes agreed that the idea of a simple note-taking and pattern-detecting app that operates completely offline using local models could be very appealing, especially since this task is the most tedious work for therapists, even if it doesn't work with insurance or requires copy-pasting reports (00:05:04) (00:07:23).
Observant Memory System and Relevance Gabor Kerekes related Amir Houieh's idea to their own experiments recording conversations and using AI to summarize them, noting that the underlying concept is a "living memory" that analyzes patterns in content (00:06:10). Amir Houieh detailed this memory as an "observant memory" that listens, memorizes, understands, and evolves over time, emphasizing that systems like RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) or large context windows cannot solve this problem because it requires continuous attention to what is relevant (00:09:44). Gabor Kerekes stressed that relevance realization is a fundamental human capacity that LLMs (Large Language Models) currently lack, necessitating the user to guide the LLM's attention to what is relevant (00:11:45).
"Learners" Architecture and Life Cycle Amir Houieh described the memory system's architecture, which includes "learners" (agents with tools and memory/understanding) that are instructed by a prompt to track specific behaviors or patterns. These learners, which store their insights in an "understanding" layer (e.g., text, graph), decide on the relevance of incoming raw data via "perceivers" and how to update the existing understanding (00:14:47). The system also incorporates a governance mechanic for the learner life cycle, allowing them to be created, merged, split, or become dormant based on factors like the number of queries they handle, ensuring the knowledge base evolves and makes obsolete learners inactive over time (00:16:48).
Implementation Status and Testing Amir Houieh presented a working prototype of a text learner, such as a sentiment tracker, which can be instructed to track the evolution of user sentiment over conversations and then queried against (00:18:09). They reported successful testing using historical data, evaluation cases, and data sets for three distinct use cases: crisis hostage reporting (tracking victims and locations via social media data), and developer memory (tracking development patterns like code and user messages) (00:19:44). Amir Houieh confirmed that the current instance of the memory is stateful and resides entirely in memory, requiring it to run as a long-running process unless persistent storage, such as storing the state in a file, is implemented (00:23:18) (00:25:45).
Deployment and Integration with Cloud Code Amir Houieh and Gabor Kerekes discussed options for deploying the memory system, with Amir Houieh suggesting a server or a CLI running in the background due to the stateful nature of the memory (00:22:20) (00:25:45). Gabor Kerekes suggested a simpler approach, proposing the memory system be packaged as a CLI tool that can be called via Cloud Code's life cycle hooks, such as when a message or conversation is finished, or using the new 'scales' feature to load context on demand (00:24:10). They agreed that the immediate next step is to extract a few days of Cloud Code history, feed it into the memory prototype, observe the results, and then figure out the integration hooks (00:27:01).
UI Development Framework Suggestions Gabor Kerekes recommended Amir Houieh consider using Datastar for building a simple UI for tracking the memory system's behavior, suggesting it offers reduced complexity compared to React and provides server-sided rendering without complex tooling (00:27:01). Gabor Kerekes explained that Datastar simplifies the process by allowing the server to directly return HTML, eliminating the need for intermediate JSON formats and complex serialization/deserialization steps common in traditional front-end ecosystems (00:28:29).
Unison Programming Language and Development Gabor Kerekes expressed excitement about the Unison programming language, which fundamentally reinvents how software is delivered by making every language construct hashable and using text only as a front-end representation of the codebase (00:31:19). This approach allows for seamless communication between different computers or between the front-end and back-end without APIs, as the code can simply be transmitted as a hash for execution (00:33:51). Gabor Kerekes views Unison as a major step forward, describing it as fixing something fundamentally broken in software composition and offering opportunities for generative UI because the back-end can generate and send Unison code for the front-end to run directly (00:36:40).
Collaborative Next Steps and Shared Memory Amir Houieh and Gabor Kerekes planned to follow up, potentially with a co-coding session soon, and Amir Houieh committed to pushing the website code (which uses NextJS) so Gabor Kerekes could continue working on it (00:38:55). Gabor Kerekes discussed the concept of a shared, common memory system built upon Amir Houieh's memory prototype, noting a strong interest in "social AI" where individual personal AI agents (with their own private contexts) could communicate with each other to derive insights for collaborative or relationship-focused applications (00:40:06) (00:41:54).
Administrative and Financial Matters Gabor Kerekes requested an update on the payment of a 2K invoice, to which Amir Houieh responded that they would take care of it within a few days, citing delays related to waiting for another payment and a cancellation (00:44:25). Gabor Kerekes reiterated their strong interest in exploring the Unison project, believing it offers a completely different, non-legacy way of building software, and noted that the company is building commercial cloud infrastructure with AI primitives on top of the open-source language (00:45:19).
Suggested next steps

Gabor Kerekes will continue or work on the website coding that Amir Houieh started this afternoon.
Amir Houieh will extract the history of cloud code for a few days, feed it into the memory system to observe the outcome, and ask cloud to make a simple UI.
Amir Houieh will push the website code so Gabor Kerekes can continue working on it.
Amir Houieh and Gabor Kerekes will try to plug some time to do a bit of V coding together tomorrow.
